To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CCDC39 is required in cilia for assembly of inner and outer dynein arm complexes, and that loss-of-function of this protein causes PCD.

we have identified the CCDC39 gene, which is required for the assembly of inner dyenins and the dyneinin regulatory complex and for ciliary motility, and that mutations in CCDC39 are a frequent cause of PCD in humans and dogs.
we have identified a new PCD locus in dogs that is caused by loss-of-function mutations of CCDC39.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes responsible for primary ciliary dyskinesis, a genetic condition which causes a number of symptoms including infertility, respiratory problems and situs inversis.
the genetic basis for human and dog primary ciliary dyskinesis.
the genetic and functional characterization of a new PCD-causing gene, CCDC38.

the genetic basis of PCD is far from complete and that additional genes will be found to cause PCD in the coming years.
